title: Felix and the Wobbling Star
markdown:
The village square of Oakhaven was, on ordinary mornings, a place of quiet chatter and the low hum of errands. On the morning of the Summer Solstice Parade it felt warm and bubbly, like lemonade left a little too long in the sun. Bunting sagged between the lampposts. Someone had polished the cobbles until they remembered they were meant to be walked on in a line.

Felix the wolf arrived with a chart rolled tight as a shy caterpillar and a hope he would not have spoken aloud to a stranger. He was a junior stargazer, keener than he was experienced, and he had spent too many thoughtful nights on the roof with a pencil and a patience that looked, from the street, like idleness. Jupiter, he was almost sure, had wobbled. Not a lurch. Not a spectacle. A difference about the size of a grain of sand, if a grain of sand could be persuaded to sit still in an almanac. The parade offered a prize for Most Ingenious Observation: a silver thimble smaller than a berry. To Felix it was a piece of the night sky that might, if he were very lucky, fit in a paw.

He did a small happy dance beside the fountain and immediately wished he had not. His heart knocked like a flustered bird. He flattened the chart against his waistcoat and tried to look like a wolf who had never danced in public.

Nearby, Bea the goat was arranging bright little flowers on a stall. She moved with a calm that made Felix's nerves look louder. "You look as if you might float away," she said, her voice like smooth pebbles in a quiet stream. "It is only a friendly parade. Mrs. Higgins will squint at anything with numbers. Mr. Abernathy likes a good loaf more than he likes a planet. They want to see you try."

Felix sighed, a small puff that took his worries with it and then brought them back. "What if my best is not clever enough? What if it is only ordinary?"

Bea chuckled, dry leaves. "Then it is ordinary, Felix. Looking at a vast quiet sky is a very good sort of ordinary."

A flurry of honks announced Bartholomew the goose. Bartholomew was a grand part of every Oakhaven parade, famous not for being perfectly right but for being wonderfully, spectacularly showy. This year he had outdone himself. A tall shining structure of brass tubes stood behind him, draped in coloured cloth and crowded with spinning glass. "Look, everyone!" he boomed, chest puffed like a small king. "The Cosmic Tuner! It turns the quiet whispers of space into music for very special ears!"

Felix's eyes left the machine and returned to his simple chart. The silver thimble receded, as if the night itself had taken a step back. Bartholomew was not merely a competitor. He was a bright, honking reminder that Oakhaven sometimes preferred looking fancy to looking carefully.

Later, Felix tried to smooth the chart, which kept curling like something shy. He heard Bartholomew talking to a cluster of young birds and field mice. "Little wobbles in planets," the goose announced, "are for those who are not quite ready for the big things. I am capturing the very heart of the universe. A peep from the moon, made large enough, becomes a concert."

Felix leaned against a cool lamppost and borrowed its solidness. His own thoughts felt like a timid whisper. A small uncomfortable feeling — envy, if he were honest — fluttered, and he tried to push it away like a stray pebble in a tidy path.

Bea came over with a crumb-covered biscuit and nudged him. "He does love an audience." Her eyes twinkled. "The stars, I think, do not need shouting. They just shine."

The words did not solve the thimble. They did, however, make the lamppost feel less like a hiding place.

The parade path, a familiar stretch of stone and flowers, filled with villagers. As the Cosmic Tuner was moved into place, a playful gust swept the square. The glass spun wildly. The cloth puffed like a ship's sails. A small important-looking piece clattered onto the stones. Villagers gasped. Bartholomew honked in surprise.

Felix felt a flutter of worry that was not only for himself. His display was a neat pile of papers tied with a bright red ribbon, and the same cheeky wind tugged at the ribbon as if it had opinions about astronomy. He caught the papers against his chest.

"We are not losing control," Bartholomew declared, voice surprisingly steady. "We are simply exploring new possibilities."

The judges — three kind villagers with thoughtful faces — went to Bartholomew first. He explained the machine with great excitement: windy air, bouncy space stuff, glass that seemed to have a mind of its own. They nodded, polite and serious.

Then their eyes turned to Felix. His heart leapt, unhelpfully. The goose's show still occupied the square like a brass weather system. Felix thought of Bea's smile, and of the steady light he had watched until his pencil went blunt. He took a breath that did not shake.

"Good afternoon," he said, and his voice came out clear. "I have been watching Jupiter. It seemed to move a tiny bit differently from what the books say. The difference was very small — about a grain of sand. It made me wonder whether the universe is more surprising than we think. There are no fireworks. Only quiet numbers. I think the numbers are interesting."

He pointed to the chart. The lines were neat. They did not spin.

A hush settled, broken by a distant bird. The judges leaned in. Polite interest became curiosity. They looked from chart to papers.

Mrs. Higgins spoke first, soft and clear. "Wonderfully clear, Felix. And accurate. We can see the work."

Mr. Abernathy, whose hands smelled of warm bread, nodded. "It takes a sharp eye to see such a small thing. And a steady hand to show it plainly."

When the awards were given, Felix had already prepared a quiet disappointment. He heard his name anyway. The silver thimble was set in his paw. It was not a concert. It was not a light show. It was a small honest discovery, offered without brass.

The setting sun caught the thimble and made a little warm coin of it. Felix did not dance. He stood in the square that still smelled faintly of lemonade and brass polish, and the night, which had not needed shouting, seemed to come a step closer after all.
characters: Felix (a wolf junior astronomer), Bea (the goat flatmate)
